title: Context Managers
prompt_markdown: Which statement safely closes files automatically?

content.explanation: The with statement handles resource cleanup.

title: Encoding
prompt_markdown: Why should you specify encoding when opening a file?

content.reference_answer: To ensure platform independence since different operating systems have different default encodings.

title: Context manager file guarantee
prompt_markdown: What is the primary architectural advantage of using `with open(...) as f:` over calling `f = open(...)` and `f.close()`?
hints: What happens if an exception occurs mid-write?

choices: It automatically compresses the file upon exit.
It guarantees `f.close()` is called even if an unhandled exception is raised inside the block.
It bypasses OS file locking mechanisms.
content.explanation: The context manager invokes `__exit__`, which ensures the file descriptor is released and buffers flushed even when unexpected exceptions occur.

title: Pathlib Path composition
prompt_markdown: Using `pathlib.Path`, what operator is used to construct path subdirectories in a cross-platform manner?

content.explanation: `pathlib.Path` overloads the `/` division operator (e.g. `Path("/var") / "log" / "app.log"`) to join path components cleanly regardless of OS separators.

title: Processing Massive Files in Memory
prompt_markdown: How should an engineer process a 50GB log file on a server with only 4GB of RAM without crashing with an OutOfMemoryError?
hints: Do not use read() or readlines().

rubric: Explains iterating line-by-line over the file object directly (`for line in f:`).
Mentions that file objects are lazy iterators that buffer only a chunk at a time.
content.reference_answer: Never use `f.read()` or `f.readlines()`, which read the entire file into memory at once. Instead, stream the file line-by-line by iterating over the file handle directly: `for line in f: process(line)`. In Python, the file object is a generator/iterator that reads from disk in small buffered chunks, consuming minimal RAM.

title: Encoding Pitfalls in Python 3
prompt_markdown: Why should code always specify `encoding="utf-8"` when calling `open()`, rather than relying on default system behavior?
hints: Consider Windows vs Linux default encodings.

rubric: Mentions that default encoding depends on platform (e.g. cp1252 on Windows vs UTF-8 on Linux).
Explains that omitting encoding causes UnicodeDecodeError or silent data corruption across deployment environments.
content.reference_answer: In Python prior to PEP 686 (Python 3.15), `open()` defaults to the system locale encoding (e.g. CP1252 on Windows, UTF-8 on Linux). If an application written on Linux runs on Windows, reading UTF-8 characters will raise `UnicodeDecodeError` or corrupt data. Explicitly specifying `encoding="utf-8"` guarantees identical, deterministic behavior across all OS environments.
